section_1.title: Intuitive Prerequisite: The Antipodal Mapping
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of a sphere (S²) and the idea of 'antipodal points'—two points exactly opposite each other. Visualize this as North and South poles, or any two points x and -x.
section_1.example: An animation showing a globe where if you touch a point in Tokyo, the corresponding antipodal point is in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.

section_2.title: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem
section_2.content: State the core theorem: Any continuous function from an n-sphere to n-dimensional Euclidean space must map at least one pair of antipodal points to the same value. Use a 'Temperature/Pressure' analogy.
section_2.example: Visualizing a map of the Earth: At any given time, there must be at least two antipodal points on the surface with the exact same temperature and air pressure.

section_3.title: Transition: The Necklace Problem
section_3.content: Define the 'Stolen Necklace' problem: Two thieves steal a necklace with k types of beads. How can they cut the necklace to divide the beads fairly (each getting exactly half of each type)? Introduce the concept of a 'discrete' problem mapped to a 'continuous' sphere.
section_3.example: A colorful necklace with 10 red beads and 10 blue beads. The goal is to cut the string into segments so that both thieves end up with 5 red and 5 blue beads.

section_4.title: The Mathematical Bridge
section_4.content: Explain how the discrete necklace arrangement is embedded into a continuous space. By modeling the possible cuts as points on a sphere, the fair distribution becomes a 'zero-sum' function that satisfies the Borsuk-Ulam condition.
section_4.example: Animation showing the necklace being stretched into a line, then wrapped around a sphere where the 'cuts' are coordinates on the sphere's surface.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Application
section_5.content: Summarize how a deep topological result provides a concrete algorithmic solution for resource sharing. Emphasize that fair division is mathematically guaranteed by the curvature of space.
section_5.example: A final visual of two characters, Alice and Bob, perfectly splitting a 'necklace' of resources using a pair of scissors, representing the Borsuk-Ulam solution.
